title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the tale to the paragraph

questions.prompt: Finish this sentence so that its second half is something the first half actually produced: "The instructions were so clear that ___"

options.text: not one of the twenty volunteers had to ask a second question
the volunteers read them three times before they understood
the manager had printed them on green paper that same morning
the volunteers were asked to come back again the following week

questions.explanation: The test is a simple one: could the degree named in the first half bring the second half about? Clarity pushed far enough leaves nobody with anything to ask, so the questions that never came are its consequence. Reading something three times before grasping it is what unclear instructions produce, and the sentence contradicts itself. The colour of the paper and the hour it was printed happened earlier and could not be caused by anything in the first half. And a second visit the following week may well be true, but no amount of clarity could ever produce it — which is exactly the trap: a fact that follows in time is not a fact that follows from a cause.

questions.prompt: A writer sets down her grandmother's real journey from Gafsa to Tunis in 1956. Every date and every place in it is true, but she supplies the talk herself, since nobody wrote any of it down. What kind of narrative has she produced?

options.text: a wholly factual one, since invented talk changes nothing
a wholly imaginary one, since one invented line taints it all
no narrative at all, since the two kinds may never be mixed
a mixture of the factual and the imaginary, which is usual

questions.explanation: Narratives come in three kinds and the third is the one people forget: imaginary, factual, or both at once. A journey whose dates and places are true and whose conversations are supplied by the writer is the ordinary shape of the third kind, and it is no fault — historical narratives are written that way all the time. Calling it wholly factual ignores pages of talk that nobody ever said. Calling it wholly imaginary throws away a real journey with real dates. And the rule that the two may never be mixed does not exist; it is the reader's job to know which half is which, not the writer's job to choose one.

questions.prompt: Two lines of your summary read: "The guide went down the valley to fetch help." and "___ the two climbers kept the injured man warm under a sheet of plastic." Which word joins them so that the reader sees both things happening at once?

options.text: In the end,
At first,
Meanwhile,
Soon afterwards,

questions.explanation: Only one connector in English puts two events side by side in time and in different places, and that is what the mountain needs: the guide is walking down while the others are keeping the man alive up above. The two connectors of sequence both destroy that: one of them makes the warming begin after the guide has already gone, and the other pushes it to the close of the whole episode, as though nobody had done anything for hours. Opening with a connector of beginning is worse still, since it turns the second line into the situation the summary starts from, when in fact it answers the first.

questions.prompt: A tale calls one of the king's counsellors an evil man. Which reading of the word is the right one?

options.text: he does harm on purpose, and is not sorry for it afterwards
he is often in a bad temper with the servants of the house
he brings bad luck to everyone who happens to stand near him
he breaks small rules whenever he thinks nobody is watching

questions.explanation: This is one of the strongest words the language has for a person, and two things make it strong: the harm is deliberate, and there is no regret behind it. Everything weaker fails. A bad temper is a fault of manner and may go with a kind man; the word would be absurdly heavy for it. Bringing misfortune to those nearby makes the counsellor unlucky rather than wicked, and luck is something that happens to a person, not something he chooses. And breaking small rules unobserved is dishonesty on a small scale, which is why English has milder words for it and keeps this one for a different order of harm.

questions.prompt: In which of these sentences does "unfaithfulness" carry the meaning this lesson gives it?

options.text: The unfaithfulness of the old clock made the whole household late.
The porter's unfaithfulness kept him in the same house for forty years.
The unfaithfulness of that summer's weather ruined the year's harvest.
The king had his queen shut away for unfaithfulness, and heard no one.

questions.explanation: In the vocabulary of this lesson the word names one thing only: being untrue to the person you are married to. That is why the accusation against a queen fits it and the three others do not. A clock that gains or loses and a summer whose weather cannot be relied on are unreliable, which is a different idea altogether and a different word in English. The porter's sentence is stranger still: staying with one household for forty years is the very picture of loyalty, so the noun there contradicts what the rest of the sentence says.

questions.prompt: Read this story. "The night train from Tunis left two hours late, and the buffet car had run out of everything but almonds. In carriage four a woman saw that the man opposite had her own suitcase at his feet, and said nothing for an hour. At Sousse she asked him, in front of the whole carriage, to open it. He opened it: it held nothing but his own tools. She apologised, he laughed, and the two of them shared a taxi from the station." Which of these has no place in a five-line summary of it?

options.text: her demand, in front of the whole carriage, that he open it
the buffet car that had nothing left in it but almonds
her belief that the case at his feet was her own
the apology, and the taxi the two of them shared

questions.explanation: Take each item away in turn and see whether the story still stands. Remove the empty buffet and nothing changes at all: it was put there to make the carriage feel real, and detail of that kind is the first thing a summary drops. Remove any of the other three and the story collapses. What she believed about the case is the trouble that starts everything; the public demand is the point of highest tension, where matters have to turn; and the apology with the shared taxi is how it is all settled. Five lines is room enough for those three and for the journey they happen on, and for nothing else.
